CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: China should announce retaliatory tariffs on the proposed U.S. list, specifically targeting politically sensitive sectors like soybeans, automobiles, and aircraft, while signaling willingness to negotiate if the U.S. de-escalates. This maintains deterrence and demonstrates resolve without foreclosing diplomatic channels.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to China is significant but not yet existential. The U.S. has proposed tariffs on up to $153 billion of Chinese imports (CBS News, April 6 2018), targeting high-tech sectors central to Made in China 2025 — 84% of the U.S. list covers high-end exports (Bruegel analysis). However, Larry Kudlow stated 'nothing's happened, nothing's been executed' and the public comment period runs until May 11, meaning these are still proposals. China's own retaliation list of $50 billion on 106 U.S. products (Reuters, April 2) has already been announced, targeting soybeans, aircraft, and autos — sectors representing 29% of U.S. exports to China. The U.S. trade deficit with China was $375 billion in 2017 (Yahoo Finance), giving the U.S. significant leverage. China's retaliation is justified because: (1) the U.S. Section 301 investigation is explicitly aimed at constraining China's technological ascent, not just trade balance (Bruegel); (2) China has already demonstrated it can target politically sensitive U.S. sectors — soybean prices fell to two-year lows after China's list was announced (CBS News); (3) semiconductors were deliberately exempted from China's retaliation list due to 'irreplaceable nature' (Bruegel), showing strategic calibration. The action_score of -1.0 reflects the need to match U.S. escalation tit-for-tat to maintain credibility, as the Global Times warned that if the U.S. thought China 'would not retaliate or would only take symbolic countermeasures, it could say goodbye to that delusion' (Reuters).

84% of U.S. tariff list covers high-end exports (Bruegel analysis)
China's $50B retaliation list already announced targeting politically sensitive U.S. sectors (soybeans, aircraft, autos)
U.S. trade deficit with China was $375B in 2017, giving U.S. significant leverage
Section 301 investigation explicitly aimed at constraining China's technological ascent
Semiconductors deliberately exempted from China's retaliation showing strategic calibration
Kudlow stated tariffs are still proposals with May 11 comment deadline
Soybean prices fell to two-year lows after China's retaliation list announced

sources_cited.excerpt: The U.S. could put tariffs on up to $153 billion of goods from China. Trump said he would consider adding another $100 billion worth of products to the list. The public has until May 11 to submit comments.

China has increased tariffs by up to 25 percent on 128 U.S. products. 'If the United States had thought China would not retaliate or would only take symbolic countermeasures, it could say goodbye to that delusion.'

84 percent of the total value of the products are high-end exports. The U.S. is not really targeting the bilateral trade deficit with China, but trying to constrain China from climbing higher up the technological ladder. Semiconductors have been exempted probably due to the irreplaceable nature.
The trade deficit with China was a record $375 billion in 2017. Trump's tariff imposition is anticipated to shrink that amount significantly, resulting in collapse of businesses and job losses.
